Entries.SourceTerm: 富嫌千口少、貧恨一身多

Senses.PreferredTarget: the rich resent a thousand mouths as too few, the poor resent one body as too many
SearchAliases: the rich resent a thousand mouths as too few, the poor resent one body as too many
Senses.Note: The rich resent a thousand mouths as too few; the poor resent one body as too many contrasts appetite amid wealth with burden amid poverty. Wuzu Fayan speaks the complete proverb in his farewell; Hongzhi Zhengjue and Dahui Zonggao reuse it as an appraisal; Baoning Renyong closes another address with it.

RelatedMasters: 三祖商那和修尊者亦名舍那婆斯
Senses.Explanation: Purna is the named interlocutor in inherited exchanges that Chan masters quote when asking how appearances and distinctions arise. Dahui invokes Purna as one who clings to appearances while disputing nature, and Yongming Yanshou also names him as foremost in exposition; a different arhat merely sharing the name was removed.

Senses.Explanation: A heading for observances held on the morning of a named master's death anniversary. One heading introduces an address on the anniversary morning of Dongshan; another labels incense offered on an anniversary morning. A third announces offerings on the anniversary morning of the old master Gaofeng at Fayusi.

AlternateTargets: a mound shaped like a bowl mold
Senses.Explanation: A small rounded mound likened to the mold over which a bowl is formed. Jue'an Kexiang, Xueyan Zuqin, and Liao'an Qingyu use the place-image independently in recorded sayings.
Senses.Note: The graph sequence names the ordinary rounded landform; no retained higher-tier passage defines it as a separate doctrinal object.
